main.title: Super Mario Bros.: The Lost Levels
main.summary: Super Mario Bros. 2, known outside of Japan as Super Mario Bros.: The Lost Levels, is a 1986 platform game developed by Nintendo R&D4 for the Famicom Disk System.

cards.text: Super Mario Bros. 2, known outside of Japan as Super Mario Bros.: The Lost Levels, is a 1986 platform game developed by Nintendo R&D4 for the Famicom Disk System. Like its predecessor, Super Mario Bros., players control Mario or Luigi to rescue Princess Peach from Bowser. The Lost Levels has a higher difficulty level, introducing obstacles such as the Poison Mushroom, counterproductive level warps and mid-air wind gusts. Luigi controls differently from Mario, with reduced ground friction and increased jump height. The game contains 32 levels across eight worlds, and 20 bonus levels.

Nintendo developed The Lost Levels after designing some of its levels for the Nintendo VS. System version of Super Mario Bros. It was directed by Takashi Tezuka and designed for players who had mastered the original. Nintendo released it as Super Mario Bros. 2 in Japan on June 3, 1986, but Nintendo of America deemed it too difficult for the North American market and released an alternative Super Mario Bros. 2 (1988) instead. The original Super Mario Bros. 2 was retitled The Lost Levels for its inclusion in the 1993 Super Nintendo Entertainment System compilation Super Mario All-Stars, its first international release. It has been rereleased for Game Boy Color, Game Boy Advance, Wii, Wii U, Nintendo 3DS, and Nintendo Switch.

Reviewers viewed The Lost Levels as an extension of Super Mario Bros, especially its difficulty progression, and appreciated the challenge when spectating speedruns. The Lost Levels gave Luigi his first unique character traits, while the poison mushroom became a recurring Mario franchise element. The Lost Levels was the bestselling FDS game, selling about 2.5 million copies. It is remembered as among the most difficult Nintendo games and recognized as a precursor to the Kaizo subculture, in which fans create and share ROM hacks featuring nearly impossible levels.

cards.heading: Super Mario Bros. 2 Turns Familiarity into a Test for Experts
cards.text: On June 3, 1986 Nintendo released the direct sequel to Super Mario Bros. in Japan for the Famicom Disk System. In the West it later became known as The Lost Levels. The graphics look reassuring, but the design starts from players' accumulated skill and turns it against them: stricter jumps, poison mushrooms, wind and deceptive trajectories turn familiar rules into an advanced course in reading space.

cards.heading: New levels for experienced Mario players
cards.text: In late 1985, during simultaneous development of The Legend of Zelda (1986), the Super Mario Bros. team began creating a version of the game for Nintendo's coin-operated arcade machine, the VS. System–while also experimenting with new, challenging level designs. They enjoyed these new levels, and thought that Super Mario devotees would too. Shigeru Miyamoto, who created the Mario franchise and directed Super Mario Bros., no longer had time to design games by himself, given his responsibilities leading Nintendo's Nintendo R&D4 division and their work on The Legend of Zelda. The Super Mario sequel was delegated to its predecessor's assistant director, Takashi Tezuka, as his directorial debut. He worked with Miyamoto and the R&D4 team to develop a sequel based on the same underlying technology, including some levels directly from Vs. Super Mario Bros. Development of the Super Mario sequel began in January 1986 and lasted about four months.

cards.heading: Mario and Luigi move differently
cards.text: The Lost Levels is a 2D side-scrolling platform game similar in style and gameplay to the original 1985 Super Mario Bros., save for an increase in difficulty. As in the original, Mario (or Luigi) ventures to rescue the Princess from Bowser. The player jumps between platforms, avoids enemies and obstacles, finds secrets (such as backwards Warp Zones and vertical vines) and collects power-ups such as the Mushroom (which makes Mario grow), the Fire Flower (which lets Mario throw fireballs), and the Invincibility Star. Unlike the original, there is no two-player mode; however, at the title screen, the player chooses between Mario or Luigi. Their abilities are differentiated for the first time: Luigi, designed for skilled players, has slower acceleration and deceleration with a higher jump height, while Mario is the opposite; he has faster acceleration and deceleration, but has a lower jump height.

cards.heading: Poison Mushrooms, wind and deceptive routes
cards.text: The Lost Levels continues the difficulty progression from Super Mario Bros. It introduces obstacles including Poison Mushrooms, warps that return the player to previous levels, and gusts that redirect the player midair. The Poison Mushroom, in particular, works as an anti-mushroom, shrinking or killing the player character. Some levels require "split-second" precision and others require the player to jump on invisible blocks. After each boss fight, Toad tells Mario that "[their] princess is in another castle". The main game has 32 levels across eight worlds and five bonus worlds. A hidden World 9 is accessible if the player does not use a Warp Zone. Bonus worlds A through D are accessible when the player plays through the game eight times, for a total of 52 levels.

main.title: Star Soldier
main.subtitle: Star Soldier Compresses Shooter Spectacle into a Test of Rhythm and Score
main.summary: On June 13, 1986 Hudson Soft released Star Soldier for Famicom.

cards.heading: Star Soldier Compresses Shooter Spectacle into a Test of Rhythm and Score
cards.text: Hudson Soft released Star Soldier for the Famicom on June 13, 1986. Its vertically scrolling stages combine rapid firing, enemy patterns and opportunities to improve a score. In Japan, the game also became associated with Caravan timed competitions, where players compared their performance within a fixed session.

cards.heading: Piloting Caesar through sixteen stages
cards.text: Players pilot the space fighter Caesar through sixteen vertically scrolling stages. A single firing attack hits both airborne and ground targets approaching from above. Background structures sometimes overlap the ship, making the route through the station part of avoiding enemy fire.

cards.heading: Flying under the station and finding capsules
cards.text: With the scrolling background of the space station, the player may occasionally enter the "trap zone", an area where the ship can fly underneath the space station to avoid enemy fire. Shooting the "P-mark" that appears in the stages can reward the player with a capsule, a power-up that increases the power of the ship's bullets as more capsules are collected. If the capsule is not collected, the ship will move slower and only shoot one bullet at a time.

cards.heading: More firing directions, a shield and Starbrain
cards.text: If two capsules are collected, the ship will transform and can be able to shoot from behind. If the player collects three capsules, the ship will start shooting in five directions and will summon a shield that protects the player until the ship is hit five times, with the fourth and final capsule collected being able to destroy any flying enemies. Starbrain appears as the boss fight at the end of each stage, with Big Starbrain, a harder variant of Starbrain, appearing in levels four, eight, twelve, and sixteen.

main.title: Ganbare Goemon! Karakuri Dōchū
main.summary: Konami brings Goemon to the Famicom and home computers. The 1986 adventure becomes the first home-system entry in the Japanese series later known internationally as Mystical Ninja.

cards.heading: Goemon comes to the Famicom
cards.text: Ganbare Goemon! Karakuri Dōchū is a video game produced by Konami. It is the second game in the Ganbare Goemon series (sometimes known in English as Mystical Ninja) and the first to be released on a video game console and home computer. It was initially released for the Family Computer on July 30, 1986 and later released for the MSX2 a year later.

cards.heading: Returning to the original adventure
cards.text: The Famicom version was re-released in Japan only for the Game Boy Advance under the Famicom Mini label and for the Wii, Nintendo 3DS and Wii U under the Virtual Console service. The game is set to be re-released in 2026 via the Ganbare Goemon! Daishūgō compilation. A direct sequel, Ganbare Goemon 2, was released for the Famicom on January 4, 1989.

main.title: Metroid
main.subtitle: Metroid Turns a Labyrinth into a Memory the Player Must Build
main.summary: On August 6, 1986 Metroid debuted on the Family Computer Disk System.

cards.heading: A map that changes with Samus
cards.text: On August 6, 1986 Metroid debuted on the Family Computer Disk System. Nintendo combined side-view action with a structure that asks players to remember doors, shafts and obstacles they cannot yet cross. Each new ability does more than make Samus stronger: it changes the player's mental map by reopening places already seen. Isolation, sound and the final reveal of the protagonist's identity complete a work that would later help give a name, alongside Castlevania, to an entire family of exploration structures.

cards.heading: Returning with new abilities
cards.text: Nintendo attempted to distinguish Metroid from other games by making it a nonlinear adventure-based game, in which exploration was a crucial part of the experience. The game often requires that the player retrace steps to progress, forcing the player to scroll the screen in all directions, as with most contemporary games. Metroid is considered one of the first video games to impress a feeling of desperation and solitude on the player. Following The Legend of Zelda, Metroid helped pioneer the idea of acquiring tools to strengthen characters and help progress through the game. Until then, most ability-enhancing power-ups like the Power Shot in Gauntlet (1985) and the Starman in Super Mario Bros. offered only temporary boosts to characters, and they were not required to complete the game. In Metroid, however, items are permanent fixtures that last until the end. In particular, missiles and the ice beam are required to finish the game.

cards.heading: Exploring Zebes and hearing its world
cards.text: Metroid is an action-adventure game in which the player controls Samus Aran in sprite-rendered two-dimensional landscapes. The game takes place on the planet Zebes, a large, open-ended world with areas connected by doors and elevators. The player controls Samus as she travels through the planet's caverns and hunts Space Pirates. She begins with a weak power beam as her only weapon, and with only the ability to jump. The player explores more areas and collects power-ups that grant Samus special abilities and enhance her armor and weaponry, allowing her to enter areas that were previously inaccessible. Among the power-ups that are included in the game are the Morph Ball, which allows Samus to curl into a ball to roll into tunnels; the Bomb, which can only be used while in ball form and can open hidden floor/wall paths; and the Screw Attack, a somersaulting move that destroys enemies in its path.

cards.heading: Sound as a living organism
cards.text: Tanaka said he wanted to make a score that made players feel like they were encountering a "living organism" and had no distinction between music and sound effects. The only time a melodic theme is heard is when Mother Brain is defeated in order to give the victorious player catharsis. During the rest of the game, the melodies are more minimalistic, because Tanaka wanted the soundtrack to be the opposite of the "hummable" pop tunes found in other games at that time.

main.title: Starflight
main.subtitle: Starflight Makes a Vast Universe Out of Limited Memory
main.summary: On August 15, 1986 Starflight arrived on DOS and offered a sense of space that was startlingly large for a home computer of its era.

cards.heading: Starflight Makes a Vast Universe Out of Limited Memory
cards.text: Starflight is a space-exploration game released for DOS on August 15, 1986. Players recruit a crew, equip a ship, visit star systems and land on planets while investigating a cosmic threat. Trading resources supports further expeditions, and discoveries provide clues to the larger story. Procedural generation helped the developers populate its extensive universe within the limits of contemporary computers.

cards.heading: Scanning planets and choosing where to land
cards.text: Starflight has 270 star systems, each containing from zero to eight planets for a total of 800. All star systems can be entered and all planets landed on, though this destroys the ship if the gravity is greater than 8.0 g. The science officer can scan and analyze the planet for information about it, including its temperature, gravity, and chemical composition. When a landing is ordered, a Mercator projection map shows the topography of each planet, as well as a cursor to select a landing point. Once the ship lands, a Terrain Vehicle can be deployed to drive across the terrain, which is periodically scanned for new information, in search of minerals, lifeforms, and alien ruins. As is the case in outer space, a heads-up display monitors the Terrain Vehicle's status.

cards.heading: A crew, six posts and a ship to equip
cards.text: The player begins inside a space station called Starport orbiting the planet Arth. Here they buy and sell minerals, Endurium (fuel), and artifacts, recruit and train crew members, and upgrade parts of the ship. The player hires a crew from five species to man the ship's six posts: navigator, science officer, engineer, communications officer, doctor, and captain. A crewman's proficiency is determined by the relevant skill: a science officer with a high science skill can determine more of a planet's properties and detect aliens at a greater range, for example. Skills are increased through training, which must be purchased. One crewman can man multiple posts, but different species have different maximum skill levels. The ship is initially equipped only with engines and a limited supply of Endurium, a type of crystal used as fuel. The ship can be modified and upgraded through the purchase of weapons, armor, and shields.

cards.heading: Drawing a story network through an open universe
cards.text: Johnson was guided by his friend and office-mate Paul Reiche III, the designer of Archon, during a period where Reiche was "supposed to be working on Mail Order Monsters". Reiche advised Johnson to draft a "story network" that would highlight all the most important points of the story and list the in-game objects necessary to advance from one to the next. The designers rewrote the script multiple times. The group designed what they called a "fractal generator", which took six man-years to develop and allowed them to increase the number of planets in the game from 50 to 800. The game was one of the earliest to use procedurally-generated content for planets and everything on them. The techniques used created a type of roguelike environment on each planet, with the contents randomly distributed. The story network was also one of the earliest examples of a sandbox game design.

main.title: Bubble Bobble
main.summary: Bub and Bob trap enemies in bubbles across one hundred single-screen stages. Taito’s 1986 arcade game turns shared space, timing and cooperation into a playful system of chain reactions.

cards.heading: The original arcade adventure
cards.text: Bubble Bobble is Taito's 1986 arcade platform game, released in North America by Romstar and Europe by Electrocoin. Players guide the dragons Bub and Bob through the Cave of Monsters to rescue their girlfriends. Enemies must be trapped in bubbles and then popped, turning into bonus items when they land. Its hundred increasingly difficult stages established a series that later included Rainbow Islands and Puzzle Bobble spin-offs.

cards.heading: Bub, Bob and enemies in bubbles
cards.text: The first game in the Bubble Bobble series is the platform arcade game Bubble Bobble, originally released in September 1986 in Japan. The game puts the players in control of two dragons, a green dragon named Bub and a blue dragon named Bob, who need to save their girlfriends from a world known as the Cave of Monsters. In each level, Bub and Bob must defeat each enemy present by trapping them in bubbles blown from their mouths and then popping the bubbles. The enemies then drop bonus items when they hit the ground. There are 100 levels total, each becoming progressively more difficult. The game was designed around two-player gameplay, and so by inserting another coin the second dragon, Bob, can be controlled.

cards.heading: Home versions and extra levels
cards.text: Bubble Bobble was ported to many home video game consoles, including the Amstrad CPC, Atari ST, ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64, MS-DOS, Apple II, Amiga, Famicom Disk System, Nintendo Entertainment System, MSX2, and Master System. The Master System port featured 200 levels and was released as Final Bubble Bobble in Japan. Ports to the Game Boy in 1991 and the Game Boy Color in 1996 were released as Classic Bubble Bobble.

cards.heading: The arcade response
cards.text: Five months after release, Game Machine listed Bubble Bobble as the second most successful arcade cabinet of the month. The same publication later listed it as the fifth-highest grossing arcade cabinet in Japan of 1987.  Bubble Bobble is considered by many sources to be among the greatest video games of all time.

cards.heading: Nintendo sequels take separate paths
cards.text: Bubble Bobble Part 2 is a sequel to Bubble Bobble which had simultaneous development by different teams on the Nintendo Entertainment System and the Game Boy. This led to each version of the game having different storylines while the gameplay was largely unchanged from the original. Both versions of the game were released in 1993.

cards.heading: Robby's rescue on Game Boy
cards.text: In the Game Boy version, a character named Robby has to rescue people from a village who have been captured by a floating skull.

cards.heading: Judy's rescue on the NES
cards.text: In the NES version, Bub's friend Judy is kidnapped by a floating skull. Bub and Bob then turn into dragons and head off to save her. In addition, unlike the original Bubble Bobble, the two players must take turns playing on every other level, rather than playing the levels cooperatively as in other entries in the series. The NES version also includes three bonus games which are located after the player defeats a boss or through a certain door.

main.title: Castlevania
main.subtitle: Horror Finds a Rhythm to Learn
main.summary: On September 26, 1986, Konami released Akumajō Dracula in Japan for the Famicom Disk System, the work that would originate the series known internationally as Castlevania.

cards.heading: Simon Belmont enters Dracula's castle
cards.text: Castlevania, known in Japan as Akumajō Dracula, is a 1986 platform game developed and published by Konami. Players control Simon Belmont, descendant of a legendary vampire hunter, who enters the castle of Count Dracula to destroy him when he suddenly reappears 100 years after Simon's ancestor vanquished him.

cards.heading: The Gesture Requires Preparation
cards.text: Simon's whip takes time to extend. Starting an attack after an enemy has already drawn close may leave him exposed before the strike lands. Players must judge the approach, stop at a useful distance and commit early enough. Learning that delay makes encounters more predictable and helps determine when it is safer to move instead.

cards.heading: Distance Becomes Identity
cards.text: The whip's reach gives Simon a consistent distance from which to attack. Enemies arrive at different heights and follow different routes, so a familiar weapon still demands changes in position. Players gradually learn which approaches bring a target into range and which require waiting for another opening.

cards.heading: Spending a Possibility
cards.text: Additional weapons offer alternatives to the whip, but using them consumes a limited resource. An attack that solves the current encounter may leave less available for the next one. Collecting a different weapon also changes the available response. Players must balance the immediate advantage against what they expect further inside the castle.

cards.heading: The Castle Is a Sequence of Commitments
cards.text: Rooms, stairs and platforms change what Simon can safely do. His fixed jump trajectory makes the takeoff position important, while staircases alter his movement and responses. On a narrow platform, even a familiar enemy can become dangerous because there is less room to prepare. Learning the castle involves remembering these combinations as well as the route to each boss.

cards.heading: Horror Becomes a Vocabulary of Action
cards.text: Bats, skeletons, armour and Medusa heads bring recognisable horror figures into the castle. Their different movements matter more than their small sprites suggest: a flying enemy crossing Simon's jump needs a different response from one approaching along the floor. Distinct silhouettes help players recognise a threat quickly while choosing where to stand and when to strike.

main.title: Alex Kidd in Miracle World
main.subtitle: Before Sonic, SEGA Was Looking for Its Hero
main.summary: Alex Kidd in Miracle World is a platform game developed and published by Sega for the Master System.

cards.heading: A kingdom built from different challenges
cards.text: Alex Kidd in Miracle World is a platform game developed and published by Sega for the Master System. The player must finish levels and overcome obstacles and puzzles in both scrolling and single-screen environments. Throughout the 17 stages, Alex faces many monsters and the three henchmen of Janken the Great, before facing Janken himself.

cards.heading: Searching for a new action hero
cards.text: Sega began Miracle Land as a project closer to an action RPG, with a protagonist carrying a staff. As the designer recalled in a Sega interview, revisions produced a martial-arts hero who could punch sideways and break scenery. The team was seeking an action game for the Mark III while Super Mario Bros. was succeeding on the Famicom. Even the button layout was deliberately different, although the designer later considered that arrangement unnatural.

cards.heading: Changing the rhythm with vehicles
cards.text: Alex can swim, ride a motorcycle and pilot the Peticopter as well as run and jump. Each vehicle changes his speed and the distance needed to respond to an obstacle. Shops and usable items add decisions about spending money between platforming sections. The variety reflects the project's earlier adventure-game direction, shaped by hardware limits such as the number of sprites available for enemies.

cards.heading: Remembering rock, paper, scissors
cards.text: Some boss encounters are settled through rock-paper-scissors. The designers debated the severity of losing a life through a choice that appeared to depend on chance. The sequences actually followed predetermined patterns, making memory useful on another attempt. These encounters give the player a different kind of challenge between the movement, vehicles and purchases of the surrounding adventure.

main.title: Zanac
main.subtitle: The Screen Responds to Our Habits
main.summary: On November 28, 1986, Zanac arrives in Japan on the Famicom Disk System, published by Pony Canyon and developed by Compile.

cards.heading: The Screen Responds to Our Habits
cards.text: Compile's Zanac is a vertically scrolling shooter first developed for MSX. Pony Canyon released a substantially reworked Famicom Disk System edition in Japan on November 28, 1986. Its Automatic Level of Difficulty Control system changes enemy pressure in response to play. Eight special weapons give players different ways to handle that changing attack pattern.

cards.heading: The Game Watches How We Play
cards.text: ALC, or Automatic Level of Difficulty Control, adjusts enemy aggression during play. Firing, collecting power-ups and destroying targets can affect the pressure on screen; some targets can also reduce it. Building a stronger ship therefore interacts with the attacks the game sends back. Experienced players can learn those relationships as well as the stages themselves.

cards.heading: Eight Special Weapons, Not One Solution
cards.text: Numbered chips provide eight special weapons alongside the main gun. Some defend the ship, some pass through targets and others fire in different directions. Collecting the same number strengthens the selected weapon. Taking another number exchanges that familiar tool for a different response, making the next pickup a choice about how to face the approaching enemies.

cards.heading: A Version to Distinguish from the MSX Original
cards.text: The Famicom Disk System edition reworked the MSX game's graphics, pacing and structure. Compile adapted the shooter to Nintendo's hardware while retaining its responsive difficulty system. This version also formed part of the game's path to a later North American NES release. The November 28, 1986 date identifies this particular edition.

main.title: Kid Icarus
main.subtitle: Climbing means learning not to rush
main.summary: On December 19, 1986, Nintendo released Kid Icarus, Hikari Shinwa: Palutena no Kagami, in Japan for Famicom Disk System.

cards.heading: Climbing means learning not to rush
cards.text: Nintendo released Kid Icarus, known in Japan as Hikari Shinwa: Palutena no Kagami, for the Famicom Disk System on December 19, 1986. Pit's adventure combines platforming and shooting with shops, upgrades and maze-like fortresses. Vertical stages make falls dangerous, while other sections extend horizontally. Collected hearts buy useful items, and rescued warriors can help against fortress bosses.

cards.heading: Climbing changes the meaning of falling
cards.text: Pit climbs through vertically scrolling sections where platforms passed below him can disappear beyond the lower edge. A fall can therefore cost a life even if a platform previously stood underneath. Before jumping, players must judge the next landing and the path of nearby enemies. Horizontal stages change that rhythm, giving Pit a different arrangement of ground and hazards to cross.

cards.heading: Hearts measure purchasing power, not affection
cards.text: Hearts left by defeated enemies are currency for shops and the black market. Clearing the path also supplies resources that can be saved or spent on recovery, weapons and other items. A purchase may make the next section safer, while saving preserves the chance to afford something more useful later. Preparation depends partly on what the player earns through combat.

cards.heading: Saving a statue can change the boss fight
cards.text: Warriors from Palutena's army have been turned into statues throughout the adventure. Freeing them provides help during fortress boss battles. Exploring before the confrontation can therefore change the amount of support Pit receives when it begins. The rescued characters make the reward for that earlier action visible in the fight.
